Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM6102 : Advanced Biomaterials { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Biomaterials
Historical background and performance of biomaterials. Overview of biomaterial processing. Classification of biomaterials: metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites. New material for biomedical applications. Smart materials and shape memory alloys.
Module 2: Biomaterial-Tissue Interactions
Corrosion and biocompatibility of orthopedic implants. Biological environment, biomaterial properties affecting interactions, and host responses. Hard tissue and soft tissue interactions with biomaterials. Absorbable polymers for orthopedic repair. Osseous grafting materials for periodontal defects. Challenges in balancing biocompatibility and bioactivity, managing chronic inflammation, and degradation byproducts.
Module 3: Applications of Biomaterials
Orthopedics: Biomaterials for joint replacements, bone grafts, and absorbable polymers for fracture repair. Dental: Titanium and zirconia implants, dental cements, and biocompatible coatings. Cardiovascular: Stents, heart valves, vascular grafts, and bioresorbable materials. Soft Tissue: Polymers for wound healing, skin grafts, and biodegradable drug delivery systems. Ophthalmics: Intraocular lenses, contact lenses, and artificial corneas. Tissue Engineering: Scaffolds for regeneration and organ repair. Smart biomaterials, nanomaterials in therapy, and wearable medical devices.
Module 4: Characterization and Testing of Biomaterials
Fundamental principles and techniques for evaluating biomaterials, including tensile strength, hardness, surface morphology, and chemical composition. Overview of sterilization methods (e.g., autoclaving, ethylene oxide, gamma irradiation) and compliance with international standards (ISO, ASTM) for medical devices. Biocompatibility Testing: In Vitro: Cytotoxicity, hemocompatibility, and protein adsorption studies. In Vivo: Animal studies to assess host response, inflammation, and tissue integration. Ethics in biomaterials and implant development.
Module 5: Biomaterial Design and Product Development
Design requirements and functional specifications for biomaterials. Material selection for specific biomedical applications. Techniques for processing and fabricating biomaterials into devices. Developing prototypes for orthopedic and dental applications. Structural and mechanical performance evaluation. Iterative design and improvement based on biocompatibility testing. Smart biomaterials and drug-eluting implants. Biomaterial integration with advanced diagnostic technologies. Ethical considerations in design and production. Energy-efficient and sustainable biomaterial manufacturing processes. Case Studies: Design of advanced implants for orthopedic and dental applications. Application of shape memory alloys and ceramic scaffolds.

Course Objective

1 .

Understand the Fundamentals and Classification of Biomaterials
2 .

Discuss the concepts of surfaces & interfaces in biomaterial interactions.
3 .

Introduce new material and fabrication techniques for designing biomedical implants.
4 .

Discuss cellular and molecular aspects of host responses to biomaterials.

Course Outcome

1 .

By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Explain the historical development of biomaterials, their classification, and the role of metals, ceramics, polymers, composites, and smart materials in biomedical applications.
2. Analyze biomaterial-tissue interactions, including corrosion, host responses, and challenges related to biocompatibility and bioactivity.
3. Evaluate the selection and application of biomaterials in orthopedics, dentistry, cardiovascular systems, soft tissue engineering, and drug delivery.
4. Demonstrate knowledge of biomaterial characterization and testing, including mechanical, chemical, and biological assessments, as well as sterilization techniques.
5. Develop an understanding of biomaterial design, selection, fabrication, and product development for medical devices, integrating sustainable practices, advanced diagnostic technologies, and ethical considerations.

2 .

J.B Park, and J.D. Boonzino, Biomaterials: Principles and Application, CRC Press

4. B. D. Ratner, F. J. Schoen, A. S. Hoffman, and J. E. Lemons, Biomaterials Science: An introduction to Materials in medicine, Academic Press

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA4612 : Building Automation { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I- Intelligent buildings, smart buildings, and building automation:
Intelligent buildings, origin and history of intelligent buildings, smart building.
Module II- Building control systems:
Control theory and practices, control devices, fundamentals of control systems, evolution of direct digital control, control sequence and documentation, application of building control, modern building automation system hardware, software, and networking required for building control systems.
Assignment(s): Exercises on descriptions of building control system
Module III- Artificial lighting controls system:
Introduction to artificial lights, evolution of lamps, luminaire design, purpose of lighting inside building, lighting design layers, smart lights, smart lighting control system, case-study on smart artificial lighting control system.
Assignment(s): Exercises on designing algorithms for lighting control system
Module IV- Daylighting controls system:
Solar altitude and azimuth angle, sun-path analysis, techniques of integration of daylighting inside building, responsive façade design, case-studies on daylighting control system.
Assignment(s): Exercises on designing algorithms for controlling daylight
Module V- Thermal comfort control system:
Automation of shading control system, smart windows, smart opaque surfaces, active means of controlling conductive heat transfer across building envelop, controlling and scheduling of openings for natural ventilation, controlling and scheduling HVAC system.
Assignment(s): Exercises on designing algorithms for thermal comfort
Module VI- Fire alarm and access controls systems:
Fire lifecycle, detection technologies, fire panel technologies, input/output devices, detector & device wiring schema, fireman's telephony & talkback system, guidelines, and fire safety strategies Access control systems, access control technologies, data encryption & security, access control strategy, access controllers, biometrics, barriers, reporting & operations.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the functioning of a building automation system.
2 .

To understand the integration of building environmental controls along with life safety, security, and maintenance functions.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Ability to integrate smart building control systems in the building design process.
2. Ability to control artificial lighting inside and surrounding the building.
3. Ability to control shading devices to permit required quantities of direct and indirect solar radiation.
4. Ability to control elements on the building envelope to create thermal comfort inside the building.
5. Ability to apply the automation systems inside the building to reduce the risk of spreading fire and enhance safety and security.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE6402 : Advanced Machine Drives { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Low cost induction motor drives 6 Hours
Steady-state analysis of three phase induction motor operation from unbalanced and nonsinusoidal supply, speed control methods of cage rotor motors, speed control of wound rotor induction motors: static Scherbius drive and Kramer drive, variable frequency operation from voltage sources and current sources, closed loop control.
Module 2 :

High performance induction motor drives 15 Hours
Vector control of induction machine: Reference frame theory and transformations, induction motor model in stationary and synchronously rotating d-q reference frames, principle of vector control, direct and indirect vector control, rotor flux and stator flux orientation control, implementation of direct and indirect vector control schemes, effects of machine parameter variation on the performance of vector controlled drives, methods of flux estimation, current controlled PWM VSI with hysteresis band, synchronous frame P-I current control, stator flux orientation control, speed sensorless vector control: speed estimation through slip calculation, direct synthesis from state equations, speed adaptive flux observer, extended Kalman filter, model reference adaptive system.
Direct Torque Control of induction motor, DTC with space vector PWM, dwell time calculation.

Module 3 :

Synchronous motor drives 15 Hours
Synchronous motor drive: Review of cylindrical rotor and salient pole synchronous machine: operating principles, characteristic equations, phasor diagram, true and self-synchronous control, Brushless DC motor, load commutated inverter fed synchronous motor, constant V/f control, scalar control with unity power factor, dynamic d-q axis model.
Vector control of synchronous motor: principle, phasor diagram and scheme of control.
Permanent magnet synchronous motor: surface permanent magnet machine and interior permanent magnet motors, brushless dc drive.
Module 4 :

Special machine drives 3 Hours
Synchronous reluctance motor, switched reluctance machine, closed speed control of SRM drive.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand and apply scalar and vector control techniques on induction motor drives
2 .

To apply estimation techniques and develop sensorless vector controlled drives
3 .

To apply direct torque control technique on induction motor drives
4 .

To develop unity power factor drives and fast response vector controlled synchronous motor drives

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: At the end of the course, students will be able to create low cost, static, scalar controlled induction motor drives
2 .

CO2: At the end of the course, students will be able to develop vector controlled induction motor drives
3 .

CO3: At the end of the course, students will be able to analyze sensorless vector control of induction motor drives and estimate speed
4 .

CO4: At the end of the course, students will be able to create direct torque controlled induction motor drive
5 .

CO5: At the end of the course, students will be able to develop unity power factor drives and vector controlled synchronous motor drives
6 .

CO6: At the end of the course, students will be able to understand PMS motors, synchronous reluctance motor and SRM drives

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ER4213 : Dynamics of Atmosphere { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Inertial and Non-Inertial frames Fundamental Forces - Pressure Gradient Forces, Gravitational Force, Friction or Viscous Force Apparent forces- Centrifugal Force, Coriolis force, Effective Gravity, Relation for a vector and its time derivative for fixed and rotating frame of reference, Seven primitive equations.
Module 2 :

Momentum Equations in Cartesian, Spherical and Isobaric coordinate systems, Scale analysis of momentum equations, Geostrophic and Hydrostatic approximation, Natural Coordinate system, Equations of motion in natural coordinate system, Balanced motion- Geostropic Wind, Gradient wind, Inertial Flow, Cyclostrophic flow, Thermal Wind, Backing and Veering of winds.
Module 3 :

Continuity equation, Scale analysis of continuity equation, Horizontal divergence, Vertical motion, Continuity equation in isobaric coordinate system, Thermodynamic energy equation, Scale analysis of thermodynamic energy equation.
Module 4 :

Circulation & Vorticity, Kelvin’s Circulation Theorem, Bjerknes circulation theorem, Application to Land & Sea breeze, Vorticity equation, Scale analysis of vorticity equation, Potential Vorticity – Application to Orographic flow, Stream function and velocity potential.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduces the fundamentals of atmospheric dynamics that govern weather and climate in the tropics and mid-latitudes.
2 .

To understand the conservation and conversion of mass, momentum, energy principles in atmosphere and various force balances, and to explore various approximations/assumptions while progressing in understanding of atmospheric dynamics.
3 .

Understanding the basic concepts in fluid dynamics, such as dynamical components of the equations of motion and Lagrangian vs. Eulerian motion.
4 .

To understand the importance of friction, Earth’s rotation and atmospheric circulation in governing the flows.

Course Outcome

1 .

Understanding the relative magnitudes of the forces and accelerations present in synoptic-scale mid-latitude weather patterns.
2 .

To learn the derivation and applications of conservation of mass, momentum, energy in the atmosphere with understanding the Eulerian and Lagrangian frameworks for solving the fundamental equations.
3 .

To have a detailed, integrated knowledge of the fundamentals of atmospheric dynamics that govern weather and climate in the mid-latitudes and tropics.
4 .

Learning the limitations, approximations, and assumptions for solving the equations in a real-world scenario.
5 .

To apply the knowledge of atmospheric dynamics for practical numerical solutions.
